He was not the most intelligent man to ever live. That much may be overrated.

But his contribution to science, and therefore our understanding of the real world/universe, is unbelievable. Most inventions/ideas are not sudden strokes of brilliance, but slowly evolved over time. Generally most "inventors" we think of are just the guy who held the commercial patent. Alexander Graham Bell didn't just invent the telephone from nothing, while no one else was working on something similar. Steam engines and atmospheric engines were being sold commercially before James Watt came along and "invented" them. Most inventions/ideas come along with a bitter dispute over who officially thought it up first.

Einstein is completely different. He thought up the idea that energy and mass are interchangeable, E = mc^2, which profoundly changed almost every body of science, from geology to astronomy, and explained so many different phenomena (like radiation). It also shows that even the tiniest amount of matter has a huge amount of potential energy. A person weighing 150lbs has enough potential energy to explode with a force greater than thirty very large hydrogen bombs (about 7 x 10^18 joule). It explained how stars could burn for billions of years without racing through their fuel.

Called “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,” it is one of the most extraordinary scientific papers ever published, as much for how it was presented as for what it said. It had no footnotes or citations, contained almost no mathematics, made no mention of any work that had influenced or preceded it, and acknowledged the help of just one individual, a colleague at the patent office named Michele Besso. It was, wrote C. P. Snow, as if Einstein “had reached the conclusions by pure thought, unaided, without listening to the opinions of others. To a surprisingly large extent, that is precisely what he had done.”

Excerpt from "A Short History of Nearly Everything" by Bill Bryson
